texts.label: text
texts.orig: Objective: This study experimentally evaluated how well lay individuals could interpret and use 4 types of electronic health record (EHR) patient-facing immunization visualizations.
texts.text: Objective: This study experimentally evaluated how well lay individuals could interpret and use 4 types of electronic health record (EHR) patient-facing immunization visualizations.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Materials and Methods: Participants (n¼ 69) completed the study using a secure online survey platform. Participants viewed the same immunization information in 1 of 4 EHR-based immunization visualizations: 2 different patient portals (Epic MyChart and eClinicWorks), a downloadable EHR record, and a clinic-generated electronic letter (eLetter). Participants completed a common task, created a standard vaccine schedule form, and answered questions about their perceived workload, subjective numeracy and health literacy, demographic variables, and familiarity with the task.
texts.text: Materials and Methods: Participants (n¼ 69) completed the study using a secure online survey platform. Participants viewed the same immunization information in 1 of 4 EHR-based immunization visualizations: 2 different patient portals (Epic MyChart and eClinicWorks), a downloadable EHR record, and a clinic-generated electronic letter (eLetter). Participants completed a common task, created a standard vaccine schedule form, and answered questions about their perceived workload, subjective numeracy and health literacy, demographic variables, and familiarity with the task.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Results: The design of the immunization visualization significantly affected both task performance measures (time taken to complete the task and number of correct dates). In particular, those using Epic MyChart took significantly longer to complete the task than those using eLetter or eClinicWorks. Those using Epic MyChart entered fewer correct dates than those using the eLetter or eClinicWorks. There were no systematic statistically significant differences in task performance measures based on the numeracy, health literacy, demographic, and experience-related questions we asked.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Patients, because of legislative action, are now required to have electronic access to their personal health data in their medical record. 1 Patients can access these data in numerous ways, including via electronic health record (EHR) patient portals, downloadable personal health records, and electronic documents produced by health systems. The rates at which individuals are accessing their personal health information through patient portals are increasing substantially. Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS), a nationally representative cross-sectional survey of 22 266 (2014, 2017-2020, 2022), showed that US adults' access to online medical record more than doubled over the past 8 years. 2 There was also a stark increase during COVID, moving from 46% in 2020 to 68% in 2022.

texts.orig: For children, 1 key piece of their personal health information is their immunization data. Good data visualizations, if designed to leverage humans' quick and effective pre-attentive processing abilities (eg, differentiating colors, sizes, shapes, and spatial positions), can help individuals provide structure and organization to their perceptions, improve recall, and identify patterns. 17 While patient-facing data visualizations have been shown to help individuals understand and interpret their health data, 18 , 19 a recent systematic review found that data visualization research within healthcare has focused heavily on clinician or researcher-facing visualizations (834 clinician/researcherfacing studies vs 39-patient facing studies). 18

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In this study, we evaluated how well lay individuals could interpret and use 4 EHR patient-facing immunization visualizations to complete an immunization form (Figure 1). The 4 visualizations contained the same de-identified immu -nization information for a 5-year old child and represented realistic ways individuals can currently access immunization information electronically: 2 EHR vendor patient portals (Epic MyChart and eClinicalworks), a downloadable copy of the patient's full record, and an electronic letter generated by a clinic using EHR data. Three of the 4 immunization visualizations shown in Figure 1 are in the form of tables (ECW, Lucy, and eLetter). Leading visualization designers see tables as a key type of visualization, but note that careful choices are often omitted from the table design process. 20 Recent publications within health informatics, including a systematic review of patient-facing visualizations, largely omit tables as a key type of health data visualization. 18 , 21 , 22 The MyChart representation, while not in table format, is the most easy-toaccess immunization data provided by the EHR vendor with the highest overall market share (Epic Systems Corporation).

texts.orig: Participants used 1 of the 4 visualization-types to complete an immunization form modeled after 3 existing public health immunizations forms (Centers for Disease Control, Minne -sota Department of Health, and California Department of Public Health). The form included dates when a child received 7 immunization-types (HepB, DTap, Hib, PCV, IPV, MMR, Chickenpox, and HepA) each with multiple doses (Figure 2). Figure 2 shows the MN, CA, CDC immunization forms as exemplars, and the form we used to collect data in this study. We were limited to using an IRB-approved secure data collection tool, specifically Qualtrics or REDCap. The form used in this study is not meant to be a suggested design, but rather a secure online Qualtrics form that mimics the structure of the CDC and state forms. texts.orig: We recruited participants using Amazon Mechanical Turk (mTurk) and randomly assigned participants to see 1 of 4 visualizations. mTurk has been shown to be an effective method for recruitment in health-related and data visualization design research. 24 , 25 We over-recruited because we knew that the mTurk data would need to be screened for duplicate IP addresses, Captcha failures, and answers to a free-text question that did not make sense (all known mechanisms for cleaning mTurk data). After screening, we had complete data for 69 participants. These data were spread across the Epic patient portal (MyChart) (n ¼ 16), eClinicalWorks (ECW) patient portal (n ¼ 16), downloadable EHR summary (Lucy) (n ¼ 15), and clinic-generated letter based on EHR data (eLetter) (n ¼ 22). In a systematic review of 581 papers focus on visualization evaluation methods from 10 years of IEEE Visualization conference publications, 23 of those that included potential end users (113 of 581 studies), a large majority (92 studies) included 20 or fewer participants. Participants were dispersed geographically throughout the United States, with an additional 4 located outside of the United States.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Participants read a study information sheet within Qualtrics and chose whether to proceed. If they continued, participants were randomly shown 1 of the 4 immunization visualizations. Remotely administered studies are thought to suffer more from participant fatigue, causing participants to become tired, bored, or unmotivated. Within-subjects designs can exacerbate this problem. In this study, if participants were to complete all 4 visualizations (based on preliminary data and confirmed by our findings) their session would have lasted roughly an hour. Between the likely occurrence of fatigue, and possible carryover effects, we chose a betweensubjects design. Other published patient-facing visualization studies have used a similar between-subjects approach, randomizing participants into visualization conditions. 18

texts.orig: We measured numeracy using the 8-item Subjective Numeracy Scale (SNS). 30 , 31 The SNS is a self-report measure of numerical ability and preference (4 questions each) containing no mathematical questions and has no correct or incorrect answers, each question answered on a 6-point scale, with 6 corresponding to the highest level of numeracy. The SNS has been validated against objective numeracy measures. We assessed health literacy using Chew's 3 health literacy screening questions, "How often do you have someone help you read hospital materials?" "How confident are you filling out medical forms by yourself?," and "How often do you have problems learning about your medical condition because of difficulty understanding written information?" 32 These brief questions have been shown to be effective in detecting inadequate health literacy. texts.orig: While the task in this study might seem straightforward, successfully completing this task required 4 of the lower-level outcomes described by Ancker et al. 22 : (1) identification of relevant data (ie, finding dates), 2) discrimination (ie, identifying differences in dates), 3) categorization of data (ie, categorizing dates by immunization-type), and 4) contrast (ie, ability to order dates in chronological order). The 4 visualization designs had unique design elements that may have contributed to these performance differences, via their support (or lack of support) of these lower-level outcomes. If it is not possible to auto-generate a customized form and display it to patients, we suggest several design principles that patientfacing immunization visualizations should abide by, all of which are supported by known design guidelines and comments from participants.

texts.orig: We did not purposively sample participants based on demographic characteristics. Given the significant differences in performance across the 4 visualizations, future research should examine whether these differences are consistent across individuals from a more diverse sample. texts.orig: The remote nature of our study caused some limitations. We could not view what participants were doing as they completed the task and we could not conduct debriefing interviews. Given that remotely administered studies are thought to suffer more from participant fatigue and the relatively long time taken to complete each task, we focused on the situation where the individual was up-to-date on their schedule. Future work should identify whether these differences exist in a situation where an individual is not up-to-date on their vaccinations.

texts.text: Conclusion

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This study demonstrated that the choice of immunization visualization design significantly affects individuals' performance completing a common task, measured by task time and accuracy. There was no difference in perceived workload across visualization designs. Based on our findings, we provided several practical guidelines for the design of immunization visualizations. Future research should focus on understanding the contexts of use and design elements that make tables an effective type of health data visualization.
